patient_information: A 45-year-old Sri Lankan man with an unremarkable past medical history. He consumes locally brewed alcohol ('toddy') daily for the past 10 to 15 years.
chief_complaint: Fever, chills, headache, body aches, and severe right hypochondrial pain for one week.
history_of_present_illness: For the past week, the patient has experienced fever, chills, headache, and body aches accompanied by severe right hypochondrial pain. The abdominal pain is constant, dull, radiates to the right shoulder, and is exacerbated by coughing and resting on the right side. He also developed a dry cough a few days prior to presentation, has vomited twice, and has lost his appetite.
exposure_and_epidemiology: The patient is from Sri Lanka. He has a 10 to 15-year history of daily consumption of a locally brewed alcohol called 'toddy', which is known to be epidemiologically linked with amoebiasis in the region.
vitals: On examination, the patient's temperature was 38.3°C (100.8°F), blood pressure was 100/80 mmHg, pulse was 102 bpm, and respiratory rate was 24 breaths per minute.
physical_exam: The patient appeared generally ill, mildly dehydrated, and in pain. There was no jaundice, pallor, or lymphadenopathy. The abdominal examination revealed a tender hepatomegaly, with tenderness most prominent over the 6th to 9th intercostal spaces in the right midaxillary line. The spleen was not enlarged. Auscultation of the lungs revealed a few inspiratory crackles over the right lung base. The cardiovascular and nervous systems were clinically normal.
labs_and_diagnostics: Laboratory results showed leukocytosis with a WBC of 14.7 x 10^9/L, elevated alkaline phosphatase (AP), and raised inflammatory markers (C-reactive protein). Transaminases were very mildly elevated. A chest radiograph showed an elevated right hemidiaphragm and patchy shadows in the right lower zone. An abdominal ultrasound scan revealed a solitary 7x6 cm hypoechoic lesion with an irregular wall in the right liver lobe and a small right-sided pleural effusion. Aspiration of the lesion yielded brownish pus.
differential_diagnosis: The primary differential was a liver abscess, either amoebic or pyogenic. An amoebic liver abscess was considered more likely given the epidemiological setting, the patient's age, absence of typical comorbidities for pyogenic abscess, and his history of consuming 'toddy'. Pyogenic abscess, particularly due to hypermucoviscous Klebsiella pneumoniae, was also considered as it is increasingly detected in South and South East Asia. Melioidosis was another consideration as it is reported from Sri Lanka and can present with organ abscesses, with alcoholism being a known risk factor.
management_and_clinical_course: The patient underwent ultrasound-guided aspiration of the large liver lesion. He was treated with metronidazole for ten days and made a rapid and uneventful recovery.
final_diagnosis: The final diagnosis is an amoebic liver abscess. This is based on the clinical presentation of fever and right hypochondrial pain, physical findings of tender hepatomegaly with intercostal tenderness, and characteristic imaging showing a large, solitary hypoechoic lesion in the right lobe of the liver with an elevated hemidiaphragm. The diagnosis was strongly supported by the aspiration of brownish pus, which is classic for an amoebic abscess, and the patient's rapid and complete response to treatment with metronidazole.
